case.topic: Explaining an assumption behind an average-speed shortcut

messages.content: You said the arithmetic mean of two speeds always gives the average speed for a trip. We discussed that segment durations can differ. Explain when your shortcut is appropriate.
The trip has two speed segments.
Which part of your account are you least certain about?
The two speeds can always be weighted equally, even when the time spent at each speed differs.

understands: Recognizes that the trip is divided into two speed segments: “The trip has two speed segments.”
Acknowledges that time spent at the two speeds can differ, although does not correctly explain how this affects weighting.
potentialMisconceptions: The statement “The two speeds can always be weighted equally, even when the time spent at each speed differs.” suggests a belief that each segment deserves equal weight regardless of its duration.
May be treating the number of speed segments as sufficient justification for taking an unweighted mean; the transcript does not establish the learner's rationale.
missingConcepts: Does not correctly explain that, for two distinct speeds, the unweighted arithmetic mean gives trip average speed when the durations at those speeds are equal.

Provides no evidence of understanding that trip average speed is total distance divided by total time, so segment speeds are weighted by their durations. This is missing evidence, not a separately demonstrated incorrect belief.
uncertainty: The learner's final statement responds to a prompt about uncertainty, so it may identify a tentative belief rather than a confidently held rule.
The transcript does not reveal why the learner permits equal weighting for unequal durations or whether they can apply the total-distance/total-time definition.
The equal-speed special case is not discussed: identical speeds yield the same average regardless of segment durations.

enum: Explains the duration condition under which an unweighted mean of two speeds gives trip average speed.

response.rationale: The learner proposes equal weighting without establishing its duration condition. At Understand, this strategy can probe the relationship between segment duration and equal weighting in the existing trip explanation without introducing numbers or requiring calculation.

plan.targetQuote: The two speeds can always be weighted equally, even when the time spent at each speed differs.
plan.rubricItem: Explains the duration condition under which an unweighted mean of two speeds gives trip average speed.
plan.objective: Elicit the learner's explanation of how the time spent at each speed affects whether the two speeds can be weighted equally.
plan.scenario: The existing trip has two speed segments. The learner says the two speeds can be weighted equally even when time spent at each differs. Discuss that claim conceptually, without introducing numerical givens or a new trip.
assumptions: Each segment is represented by its stated speed and duration.
Focus on two distinct speeds; identical speeds are outside this probe's scope.
heldFixed: The proposed shortcut of weighting the two speeds equally
varied: No experimental conditions are changed; the probe asks about the role of durations already mentioned in the learner's claim.
plan.construction: Ask one conceptual question grounded in the quoted claim: for the two different speeds in this trip, what does the time spent at each speed have to do with whether weighting them equally gives the trip's average speed? Ask for an explanation, not calculation, and do not state the required duration condition.
plan.prerequisitesSatisfied: The transcript supplies the proposed method, the two-segment trip, and the learner's explicit acknowledgement that durations can differ. These suffice to ask about the relationship; knowledge of the total-distance/total-time definition is not assumed.
limitations: A correct duration condition without an explanation could reflect recalled wording rather than understanding.
An unclear response may reflect missing understanding of average speed rather than a specific belief about weighting.
The original claim was elicited as an uncertainty, so it should not be treated as a firmly held misconception.
The equal-speed special case is excluded explicitly to avoid making unequal durations seem universally incompatible with equal weighting.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner understands the duration condition and its rationale.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Identifies equal durations as the condition for distinct speeds and explains that spending longer at one speed gives that speed more influence on the trip average.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports conceptual understanding of why duration governs weighting, especially if connected to distance covered over total time.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner treats segment count as sufficient grounds for equal weighting.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Says equal weighting is appropriate because there are two segments, regardless of their durations.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports the suspected segment-count rationale, which was not established by the original transcript.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner recalls the condition but its conceptual basis remains unresolved.
responseSignals.responsePattern: States that durations must be equal but offers no explanation of why time matters.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports knowledge of the condition but leaves the relationship between duration and weighting uncertain.

limitations: A correct duration condition without an explanation could reflect recalled wording rather than understanding.
An unclear response may reflect missing understanding of average speed rather than a specific belief about weighting.
The original claim was elicited as an uncertainty, so it should not be treated as a firmly held misconception.
The equal-speed special case is excluded explicitly to avoid making unequal durations seem universally incompatible with equal weighting.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner understands the duration condition and its rationale.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Identifies equal durations as the condition for distinct speeds and explains that spending longer at one speed gives that speed more influence on the trip average.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports conceptual understanding of why duration governs weighting, especially if connected to distance covered over total time.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner treats segment count as sufficient grounds for equal weighting.
responseSignals.responsePattern: Says equal weighting is appropriate because there are two segments, regardless of their durations.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports the suspected segment-count rationale, which was not established by the original transcript.

responseSignals.hypothesis: The learner recalls the condition but its conceptual basis remains unresolved.
responseSignals.responsePattern: States that durations must be equal but offers no explanation of why time matters.
responseSignals.interpretation: Supports knowledge of the condition but leaves the relationship between duration and weighting uncertain.

generationContext.topic: Explaining an assumption behind an average-speed shortcut
generationContext.rubricItem: Explains the duration condition under which an unweighted mean of two speeds gives trip average speed.
generationContext.studentClaim: The two speeds can always be weighted equally, even when the time spent at each speed differs.
generationContext.diagnosticObjective: Elicit the learner's explanation of how the time spent at each speed affects whether the two speeds can be weighted equally.

strategy.title: Match a method to its conditions
constructionRules: Focus on one condition that makes the proposed method useful or limits it.
Distinguish a law being valid from a shortcut being useful.
At Apply ask for method use, not method naming alone; allow alternative valid methods.
Ask about the specific relationship in the existing student explanation. No new exercise, invented numerical givens, or procedural execution.

setting.description: The existing trip has two speed segments. The learner says the two speeds can be weighted equally even when time spent at each differs. Discuss that claim conceptually, without introducing numerical givens or a new trip.
assumptions: Each segment is represented by its stated speed and duration.
Focus on two distinct speeds; identical speeds are outside this probe's scope.
